conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’m here to help you settle into motherhood and to check on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived.

Today I’d like to do a quick, routine screen called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s a simple 10-question form that looks at mood, anxiety, and self-harm thoughts in the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting; it just gives us a snapshot of how you’re coping so we can offer the right support. Everything you share stays confidential, and we’ll move at your pace.

I’ll ask each question conversationally—no need to remember numbers or categories. When you’re ready, we can start.

Here’s the first one:

Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

Oh… yes, I still laugh. Just yesterday my husband made a goofy face while changing a diaper and I burst out laughing. It’s maybe a little harder to catch my breath because I’m tired, but the giggles are still there.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, that sounds right—I’ve still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to little things, like taking the baby for a walk in the stroller or my favorite show coming on after I put her down. It’s not every minute, but there are still moments I genuinely anticipate.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. If I’m running late or she spits up on a fresh outfit, I just think, “Well, that’s babies for you.” I don’t beat myself up about it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I do get a bit anxious sometimes—mostly about whether she’s breathing okay or if her temperature’s normal—but it’s usually when I’m checking on her at night. It doesn’t feel totally “no good reason,” because she’s so tiny and new, but I guess the worry pops up even when everything looks fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I haven’t felt scared or panicky out of nowhere. If I get a little rush of worry, it’s when I’m walking into her room and can’t hear her make a sound, but once I see her chest moving I calm right down.
Things have been getting on top of me

Now and then, yeah—like yesterday when she wanted to cluster-feed right as the groceries got delivered and the dog started barking. For a minute I thought, “How do I juggle all this?” But once I sat down to nurse, it felt manageable again.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, I’m sleeping pretty well—usually a four-hour stretch and then a couple of two-hour chunks. I’m tired, but it’s more from the night feeds than from being upset.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t felt really sad or miserable. I get a little weepy when I’m overtired, but it passes quickly and most of the time I feel okay.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I teared up once this week when she wouldn’t latch and my nipples were sore, but it was more from frustration than feeling miserable, and it stopped as soon as she finally fed.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. That hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

You're navigating the early weeks of motherhood with resilience: you still laugh with your husband, look forward to small pleasures, and quickly calm when worries pop up. The occasional <sym>anxiety</sym> you feel is tied to normal newborn vigilance and passes once you see your baby is safe, and brief moments of feeling overwhelmed resolve as soon as you sit to nurse. Overall you report good spirits, steady sleep, and no persistent sadness or self-harm thoughts.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 5, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>Patient acknowledges persistent worry that arises even when objectively things are fine, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items cluster in the minimal range (total 5). Positive findings: mild <sym>anxiety</sym> without panic (Q4=2), occasional <sym>stress</sym> when tasks collide (Q6=1), and rare tired-related weepiness (Q8=1). All core mood items are negative: preserved pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym> absent), no pervasive <sym>sadness</sym> or <sym>guilt</sym>, sleep intact, no crying spells from mood, and zero self-harm ideation. Pattern fits normal postpartum adjustment rather than <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> per <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> requiring ≥5 symptoms including low mood or anhedonia most days for two weeks. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue routine postpartum visits and re-screen if mood deteriorates
2. Practice brief breathing or grounding exercises when checking baby at night to ease residual <sym>new-mom vigilance</sym>
3. Share feelings openly with partner or peers; consider local new-parent groups for support
4. Maintain sleep hygiene: nap when baby naps and accept help with chores to reduce fatigue
5. Seek prompt evaluation if you notice persistent low mood, loss of interest, or scary thoughts
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 5: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant approx. ≤ 8 wks) – self-report EPDS-style questionnaire  

Symptoms endorsed  
• Mild, situational anxiety (Q4, Q5) – concerns center on infant safety; resolves quickly with reassurance  
• Occasional feeling of being “on top of” multiple demands (Q6) – transient, alleviated once situation stabilised  

Symptoms denied  
Loss of pleasure/enjoyment, pervasive sadness, excessive guilt, sleep disturbance secondary to mood, crying spells, self-harm ideation (Q1-3, 7-10 all negative)  

Pattern  
Overall euthymic affect; anxiety is context-specific and subsides rapidly. No evidence of persistent low mood, anhedonia, or cognitive distortions typical of major postpartum depression.  

Risk factors identified  
• Situational vigilance / health-related worries common in normative postpartum adjustment (no generalised or panic-level symptoms)  
• No current safety concerns (zero self-harm endorsement)  

Screening observation  
Findings do not indicate elevated probability for major postpartum depression or anxiety disorder at this time; presentation consistent with typical post-birth adjustment. Continue routine paediatric and maternal follow-up; re-screen if mood, anxiety, or coping deteriorate.
